name: Scott Aaronson
milestone_by_age_26: Published the quantum lower bound for the collision problem at STOC 2002 at age 21, resolving a years-old open problem in quantum computing.
early_history_summary: Aaronson became interested in quantum computing as an undergraduate at Cornell and published his first major result—the quantum lower bound for the collision problem—at age 21 while a PhD student at UC Berkeley under Umesh Vazirani. He completed his PhD at age 23 with a thesis on limits of efficient computation in the physical world.
primary_early_advantage_tags: elite university pipeline, doctoral mentor, quantum computing frontier
evidence_summary: Aaronson enrolled at Cornell at 16 and became interested in quantum computing, then moved to UC Berkeley for his PhD under Umesh Vazirani, a leading quantum computing researcher. His quantum lower bound for the collision problem, published at STOC 2002 when he was 21, resolved a significant open problem. The work was done within the elite Berkeley theoretical computer science ecosystem with direct mentorship from Vazirani. Family background is not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Schlumberger Centennial Chair of Computer Science at the University of Texas at Austin; leading researcher in quantum computing and computational complexity theory.

trajectory.event: Published quantum lower bound for the collision problem at STOC, resolving a years-old open problem in quantum computing.
Completed PhD at UC Berkeley with thesis 'Limits on Efficient Computation in the Physical World'.
Joined MIT as faculty after postdoctorates at IAS and University of Waterloo.
Received PECASE (Presidential Early Career Award for Scientists and Engineers).
Published the boson sampling result with Arkhipov, establishing a likely quantum supremacy candidate.
Received the ACM Prize in Computing.
Joined OpenAI to work on AI safety and alignment.

name: Kaiming He
milestone_by_age_26: Won the CVPR 2009 Best Paper Award for 'Single Image Haze Removal Using Dark Channel Prior' at age 24-25, the first Chinese researcher to receive this honor.
early_history_summary: He scored first place in the 2003 Guangdong provincial college entrance exam and entered Tsinghua University's elite basic science class. He interned at Microsoft Research Asia as an undergraduate and began his PhD at CUHK under Tang Xiao'ou in 2007. His first paper on dark channel prior haze removal won CVPR Best Paper in 2009.
family_context_summary: Born in Guangzhou as an only child; parents worked in enterprise management. He was sent to art classes at a young age, developing a patient and focused temperament.
parent_family_domain_summary: Parents worked in enterprise management; no direct academic or technical domain transfer documented.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Tsinghua elite program, MSRA internship, top-tier PhD advisor
evidence_summary: He entered Tsinghua University's elite basic science class after scoring first in Guangdong's provincial exam. As an undergraduate he interned at Microsoft Research Asia, gaining early access to frontier computer vision research. His PhD at CUHK under Tang Xiao'ou (founder of SenseTime) provided direct mentorship from a leading figure. His CVPR 2009 Best Paper on dark channel prior was the first by a Chinese researcher. Parents were in enterprise management, not academia.
starting_point: Born in Guangzhou to parents in enterprise management; an only child who developed focus through early art training.
current_position: Associate Professor at MIT EECS and Distinguished Scientist at Google DeepMind; creator of ResNet with 700,000+ citations.

trajectory.event: Graduated from Tsinghua University and began PhD at CUHK under Tang Xiao'ou.

name: June Huh
milestone_by_age_26: Proved the Read-Hoggar conjecture on unimodality of chromatic polynomial coefficients in 2009 at age 25-26, resolving a 40-year-old open problem in graph theory.
early_history_summary: Huh was a late bloomer who dropped out of high school to write poetry and struggled academically at Seoul National University. A chance encounter with Fields Medalist Heisuke Hironaka in his sixth year sparked his interest in math. He proved Read's conjecture in 2009 during his early PhD studies at UIUC, using algebraic geometry methods.
family_context_summary: Born in Stanford, California while parents were completing graduate school; family moved to Seoul when he was about 2. Father was a statistics professor at Korea University; mother was a professor of Russian literature at Seoul National University.
parent_family_domain_summary: Both parents were university professors—father in statistics, mother in Russian literature—providing an academic household environment, though Huh showed little early interest in math.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Hironaka mentorship, academic family, late specialization
evidence_summary: Huh was an unlikely prodigy who dropped out of high school to write poetry and struggled through six years of college. His turning point was meeting Fields Medalist Heisuke Hironaka at Seoul National University, who became his mentor and invited him to travel to Japan as a personal assistant. This sustained mentorship gave Huh access to deep mathematical thinking. Both parents were professors, providing an academic environment. He proved Read's 40-year-old conjecture in 2009 at age 25-26 during his first year of PhD studies at UIUC.
starting_point: Born in Stanford, CA to academic parents; father a statistics professor, mother a Russian literature professor; family returned to Seoul when he was 2.
current_position: Professor of Mathematics at Princeton University; Fields Medalist (2022) and MacArthur Fellow.

trajectory.event: Proved the Read-Hoggar conjecture on chromatic polynomial unimodality during early PhD studies at UIUC.
Completed PhD at University of Michigan under Mircea Mustata, winning the Sumner Byron Myers Prize.
With Adiprasito and Katz, proved the full Heron-Rota-Welsh conjecture for matroids.
Received New Horizons in Mathematics Prize.
Awarded the Fields Medal and MacArthur Fellowship for connecting algebraic geometry and combinatorics.

name: Maryna Viazovska
milestone_by_age_26: Co-authored a paper on spherical designs submitted to the Annals of Mathematics in 2011 at age 26, solving a long-standing conjecture by Korevaar and Meyer.
early_history_summary: Viazovska grew up in Kyiv and attended a specialized math and physics lyceum. She earned her bachelor's from Kyiv University and master's from Kaiserslautern before beginning her PhD at Bonn under Don Zagier. Her 2011 paper on spherical designs with Bondarenko and Radchenko was accepted at the Annals of Mathematics, the most prestigious math journal.
family_context_summary: Born in Kyiv, the oldest of three sisters. Father was a chemist at the Antonov aircraft factory; mother was an engineer. She attended a specialized science lyceum.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a chemist and mother an engineer, providing a technical household, though neither was a research mathematician.
primary_early_advantage_tags: specialized math lyceum, elite PhD advisor, Ukrainian math community
evidence_summary: Viazovska attended a specialized math-physics school in Kyiv where a former research mathematician (Andrii Knyazyuk) taught. She began collaborating with Andriy Bondarenko as an undergraduate, and their work with Danylo Radchenko on spherical designs was submitted to the Annals of Mathematics in 2011 when she was 26. Her PhD advisor Don Zagier at Bonn was a leading number theorist. Parents were a chemist and engineer in Kyiv.
starting_point: Born in Kyiv to a chemist father and engineer mother; oldest of three sisters; attended a specialized math-physics lyceum.
current_position: Full Professor and Chair of Number Theory at EPFL Lausanne; Fields Medalist (2022), only the second woman to receive the award.

trajectory.event: Co-authored paper on spherical designs submitted to Annals of Mathematics with Bondarenko and Radchenko.

name: Taylor Wilson
milestone_by_age_26: Became the youngest person to achieve controlled nuclear fusion in 2008 at age 14, using an inertial electrostatic confinement device built in a university lab.
early_history_summary: Wilson became interested in nuclear science at age 10 after reading about a teenage nuclear enthusiast. With parental support, he gained access to the University of Nevada physics lab where he built a working fusor at age 14. He later won a Thiel Fellowship and developed radiation detectors for security applications.
family_context_summary: Born in Texarkana, Arkansas to Kenneth Wilson (owner of a Coca-Cola bottling plant) and Tiffany Wilson (yoga instructor). Family had resources to support his early scientific interests.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father owned a Coca-Cola bottling plant; mother was a yoga instructor. No direct nuclear science background, but family had financial resources to support expensive hobbies.
primary_early_advantage_tags: university lab access, family financial support, early nuclear specialization
evidence_summary: Wilson's father owned a Coca-Cola bottling plant, providing financial resources for his son's expensive nuclear experiments. At age 14, with access to the University of Nevada physics lab, Wilson built a working nuclear fusion reactor (fusor), becoming the youngest person to achieve fusion. He gained significant media attention and a Thiel Fellowship. His parents actively supported his interests, facilitating lab access despite the unusual nature of a teenager working with nuclear materials.
starting_point: Born in Texarkana, Arkansas to a Coca-Cola bottling plant owner father and yoga instructor mother; family had financial resources to support his scientific interests.
current_position: Nuclear physicist and inventor; developing modular nuclear fission reactor technology; resides in Reno, Nevada.

trajectory.event: Became the youngest person to achieve controlled nuclear fusion using a fusor built at the University of Nevada.

name: Sabrina Gonzalez Pasterski
milestone_by_age_26: Co-discovered the spin memory effect in gravitational waves, published in the Journal of High Energy Physics in 2016 at age 22-23; research was cited by Stephen Hawking.
early_history_summary: Pasterski started flying lessons at age 9 and built a plane by 14. She entered MIT at 17, graduated in 3 years with a perfect 5.0 GPA in physics, and began her PhD at Harvard under Andrew Strominger. Her co-discovery of the spin memory effect was published when she was 22-23.
family_context_summary: Born in Chicago to a Cuban-American family. Her father and grandfather supported her early interest in aviation; her grandfather helped her get a Cessna aircraft kit.
parent_family_domain_summary: Family supported her early aviation interests; her father arranged for her grandfather to get her a Cessna, which she built and flew solo at age 14.
primary_early_advantage_tags: MIT physics pipeline, Strominger mentorship, early aviation building, Forbes 30 Under 30
evidence_summary: Pasterski built and flew a single-engine aircraft at age 14, which helped her gain admission to MIT despite being initially waitlisted. She graduated MIT in 3 years with a perfect 5.0 GPA, the first woman in decades to top the physics program. At Harvard, her PhD advisor Andrew Strominger and collaborator Alexander Zhiboedov helped her co-discover the spin memory effect, published in JHEP 2016 when she was 22-23. The work was cited by Stephen Hawking. She was on Forbes 30 Under 30 at age 22.
starting_point: Born in Chicago to a Cuban-American family; father and grandfather supported her early aviation interests; built and flew a plane at 14.
current_position: Faculty member at Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics; founder and PI of the Celestial Holography Initiative.

trajectory.event: Graduated from MIT with a perfect 5.0 GPA in physics, first woman in decades to top the program.

name: Brittany Wenger
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 2012 Google Science Fair Grand Prize at age 17 for building a cloud-based artificial neural network that diagnoses breast cancer with 99.1 percent sensitivity.
early_history_summary: Wenger became interested in artificial intelligence in seventh grade and taught herself programming. After her cousin was diagnosed with breast cancer, she applied neural networks to fine needle aspirate breast cancer data, building a cloud-based diagnostic tool. She won the Google Science Fair in 2012 and her program was tested in hospitals.
family_context_summary: Grew up in Sarasota, Florida. Her cousin's breast cancer diagnosis inspired her research. She taught herself programming from a book in seventh grade.
primary_early_advantage_tags: self-taught programming, cloud computing platform, personal cancer motivation
evidence_summary: Wenger taught herself programming from a book in seventh grade with no prior experience. After her cousin's breast cancer diagnosis, she built an artificial neural network using publicly available data from the University of Wisconsin, deployed on Google App Engine. Her cloud-based diagnostic tool achieved 99.1 percent sensitivity and won the 2012 Google Science Fair at age 17. She used Google's cloud platform as both a development tool and a distribution channel, and her program was later tested in hospitals in the US and Italy.

current_position: Pediatrician; former Duke University student; her cancer diagnostic software was tested in hospitals in the US and Italy.

name: Jack Andraka

The ISEF win in 2012 brought massive media attention, though later analysis showed some claims were overhyped. The sensor's clinical efficacy has not been independently validated.

parent_family_domain_summary: Mother taught engineering (fluid mechanics) at a college; father held a B.Tech and owned a ceramics company. Family had strong technical and educational orientation.
